title: Modular Terraform module for observability in VPC: decoupled OTEL collector, Prometheus/Grafana, and log relay
creator: Aditi Rao
description: Scope: Build a modular, reusable Terraform module to provision the observability stack inside customer VPCs for Private deployments. The module must support independent lifecycle and upgrade of: (1) OpenTelemetry Collector (OTEL) as a relay/proxy, (2) Prometheus and Alertmanager for metrics, (3) Grafana for dashboards, and (4) log shipping (Vector/Fluentd) to controlled sinks. Goals: idempotent deployments, minimal blast radius for upgrades, clear terraform inputs/outputs for private control plane to wire up RBAC and KMS, and automated health checks and alerting default configs. This ticket covers design, implementation, docs, and migration strategy for existing private customers.
implementation_notes: Module layout: root module 'redwood/observability/vpc' with child modules: prometheus/, grafana/, otel_collector/, log_relay/, alertmanager/, healthchecks/
Provider strategy: accept provider aliases from caller (aws, gcp) and do NOT instantiate provider blocks inside module. Use terraform >=1.6 to support for_each on modules.
State management: recommend per-environment workspaces with separate state files for core infra vs observability to allow independent upgrades.

OTEL design: run OTEL collector as a horizontally scaled service (k8s or ECS) with config templating via SSM/SecretsManager. Collector should act as a film strip: ingest -> transform -> relay to internal S3/MinIO for logs and to Concordant ingest endpoints for metrics/traces.
Prometheus: use Thanos sidecar pattern for long-term storage optionality. Expose metrics via VPC private ALB and require security group onboarding in module inputs.

Grafana: ship initial dashboards that mirror hosted Console views. Default to read-only admin with provisioned datasources pointing to Prometheus/Thanos. Support optional datasource provisioning for external S3/CloudWatch.
Log shipping: default implementation built on Vector with an option to use Fluentd. Support batching, backpressure, TLS to sinks, and KMS-wrapped credentials.
Health checks: each child module must register an HTTP/GRPC health endpoint and optional CloudWatch/Stackdriver alarms. Provide a 'observability_health' output map for the control plane to poll.

Upgrade strategy: blue/green deployments for collector and grafana with traffic cutover. Prometheus migrations require series retention considerations; provide a migration runbook and automated snapshot before major changes.
Testing: add an acceptance test suite in CI to deploy to a test VPC, validate endpoints, simulate failover, and run 'tf plan' drift tests. Use a mocked sink for logs/metrics in CI to keep costs low.
decisions: Make OTEL collector a separate child module to allow customers to run their own collector while using Redwood-managed Prometheus/Grafana.
Default to Vector for log shipping because of better memory footprint and fewer heavy ruby deps compared to Fluentd; expose 'provider' flag to switch.
Do not include managed DNS records by default; leave DNS management to customer or higher-level terraform to avoid cross-account upgrades complexity.
Expose a single boolean variable 'managed_alerting' to provision Alertmanager with reasonable defaults; defaults can be overridden by customers through templates.
All IAM/KMS resources created only when explicitly requested via 'create_iam' and 'create_kms' flags to support air-gapped/on-prem customers.
Security review required for default dashboards and any embedded API keys; sensitive outputs will be omitted and instead returned as references (SSM/SecretsManager paths).
tradeoffs: Decoupling modules increases UX surface area for customers (more variables), but significantly reduces blast radius and allows partial upgrades without downtime.
Supporting both Vector and Fluentd increases maintenance burden but is necessary for customers with established operator preferences.
Using Thanos adds operational complexity and cost; it's optional and gated behind an input flag 'enable_long_term_storage'.
progress_updates: 2026-02-12: Initial design doc published in Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/OPS/Observability+VPC+Terraform+Module (draft).
2026-02-20: Prototype OTEL child module implemented in infra-repo branch feat/observability-modular. Minimal unit tests passing. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/468
2026-02-28: Prometheus child module scaffolded; decided on Thanos optional integration. Started smoke tests in test account.
2026-03-04: Vector-based log_relay implementation completed. Ran integration tests that validated TLS to mock-s3 sink and KMS envelope encryption.

2026-03-08: First end-to-end test failed due to missing IAM permissions for cross-account metric scraping — added 'prometheus_scrape_role' variable and updated IAM docs. PR open: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/503
2026-03-09: Security sign-off requested; flagged for security review before merging to main.
acceptance_criteria: Module publishes to terraform registry under redwood/observability/v1.0.0 (draft acceptable) and includes full README with example usage.
A test VPC deployment via CI must deploy OTEL collector + Prometheus + Grafana + Vector, run health checks, and produce successful 'observability_health' output map.
Upgrade path documented: steps for minor config changes and a rollback procedure with snapshots/backups for Prometheus.
No sensitive secrets printed in TF outputs; any secret material is stored in SSM/SecretsManager and references are returned instead.
CI tests cover canary upgrade where OTEL collector is upgraded to a new image and traffic is validated against a mock payload for 10 minutes without error.
notes_for_reviewers: Please validate that the OTEL collector configuration supports both metrics and traces with minimal sample configs for common frameworks (OpenTelemetry JS/Go/Python).
IAM policy suggestions are in the design doc; security team will need to check least-privilege for cross-account scraping roles and KMS key usage.
Look for any hard-coded endpoints in dashboards that could leak internal hostnames; prefer datasource references and variables.
